The VIX closed at 35.9 on Friday’s monthly options expiration, its highest on an expiration day since April 2020.

Since 1990, there have been 30 expirations with the VIX at 30 or higher. What the S&P 500 did next (vs. all days):

▪ First week: a coin flip, higher about half the time.
▪ One month: median +4.4%, higher 77% of the time (all days +1.2%, 64%).
▪ Six months: median +17.4%, higher in 28 of 30 (all days +5.7%, 75%).
▪ The catch: the median worst close within three months was −4.9%, and in September 2008 the index fell 21.5% in a month.

Counting only the first expiration in each run (12 cases), the S&P 500 was higher six months later 11 of 12 times.

Inflation in Japan is accelerating:

Japan's CPI inflation excluding fresh food jumped +2.1% YoY in September, its highest YoY increase since December 2025.

Since May, Japan's CPI inflation has risen +0.6 percentage points.

Furthermore, CPI excluding fresh food and energy surged +2.4% YoY, its largest YoY increase since January.

Overall CPI inflation rose +2.1% YoY last month, its highest reading since November 2025.

This comes as the Iran War continues to fuel inflationary pressures in Japan, which relies heavily on imported food and energy.

Meanwhile, Japan's major food and beverage companies planned price increases for 3,153 items in October, the 2nd consecutive monthly reading above 3,000 for the first time since July 2023.

Inflationary pressures in Japan are broadening again.

BREAKING: This past week's -10.4% drop in the Nasdaq 100 was one of the rarest weekly declines in 40 years.

Of the last 2,133 trading weeks, just 11 saw declines of this magnitude or worse.

That's 0.52% of all weeks, a 3.27 standard deviation move based on the historical mean and volatility.

Of course, market returns exhibit "fat tails," meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict.

However, even accounting for the fact that extreme market moves are more common than traditional statistical models suggest, this was a historically rare selloff.

Volatility returns when markets least expect it.

The semiconductor trade is still popular among fund managers:

39% of global fund managers said "long global semiconductors" was the most crowded trade, according to a BofA survey of 169 fund managers overseeing $461 billion in assets conducted between November 6th and November 12th.

This marks the 6th consecutive month that semiconductors have held the top spot.

However, this figure is down from the 82% peak recorded in July this year.

Meanwhile, “Short China Stocks” ranked 2nd for the first time, with 14% of respondents identifying it as the most crowded trade.

By comparison, "Long Magnificent 7" and "Short Treasuries" were considered the most crowded trades just by 12% and 10% of fund managers, respectively.

Investor appetite for semiconductor stocks remains strong.
